approved: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
The bill would give law enforcement agencies stronger powers to investigate and penalise illegal tobacco activities.
It would raise criminal penalties for offences under customs, excise and tax laws, and improve the proceeds of crime regime to seize assets from illicit tobacco trading.
The explanatory memorandum states the bill does not create major new powers but clarifies and strengthens existing information-gathering and confiscation mechanisms.
Increase criminal penalties for offences related to importing, possessing, producing or selling illicit tobacco under the Customs Act, Excise Act and Taxation Administration Act.
Make the proceeds of crime regime more effective at confiscating the profits and instruments of illicit tobacco crime.
Enable broader use of investigatory powers such as computer access and surveillance for illicit tobacco offences.
Criminal actors involved in the illicit tobacco trade, law enforcement agencies, and the Australian community.

The question is that the amendment on sheet 3860 be agreed to. _One Nation's circulated amendment—_ At the end of the motion, add ", but the Senate: (a) notes that: (i) organised crime now accounts for up to 80% of sales of tobacco products, (ii) law enforcement is overwhelmed by the scale of the illicit tobacco industry leading to widespread violence and property damage, (iii) law-abiding citizens and small businesses in proximity to illicit tobacco outlets are in physical and financial danger, (iv) organised crime is facilitating cigarette sales to children, and (v) the very high rate of tobacco excise has broken the compact between the government and the public to each treat the other fairly; and (b) calls on the Government to: (i) reduce the excise rate of tobacco products by 75%, effective immediately, (ii) maintain the lower rate until organised crime has been controlled, (iii) cancel indexation of the excise rate for three years, (iv) direct the Office of the eSafety Commissioner to use their existing powers to take down websites offering direct sales of illicit tobacco products, and (v) return tobacco excise to a more sensible level once organised crime has been controlled".

Moved the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill, arguing that illicit tobacco has become a serious organised crime and public health problem; the bill would increase penalties, expand investigative and telecommunications powers, strengthen proceeds-of-crime measures and disrupt criminal profits and networks.

Criticised the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026 as inadequate to address illegal tobacco and vaping, arguing that enforcement, prosecution and a coordinated law enforcement strategy were needed. Called for legalised vapes with quality control, and linked illicit imports to serious organised crime, sex slavery, drug offences and terrorism.

Argued that high tobacco excise and enforcement-only policies had fuelled an illicit tobacco market linked to organised crime, violence and firebombings, citing 285 attacks, a market worth $6.9 billion and 55 per cent of total consumption. Called for lower excise, harm reduction, regulated vapes and stronger surveillance and penalty powers.

Supported the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026, arguing that higher penalties, broader investigative powers and proceeds-of-crime reforms would reduce the profitability of organised illicit tobacco operations, enable asset confiscation and unexplained-wealth proceedings, improve regulatory cooperation, and protect public revenue and funding for essential community services.

Supported the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026, arguing that an illicit market worth up to $6.9 billion is linked to organised crime, unsafe products and violence affecting Melbourne businesses; endorsed stronger enforcement, proceeds-of-crime measures and national coordination, while rejecting tobacco-excise cuts as a solution and warning of industry influence.

Declared that the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026, the Australia's Foreign Relations (State and Territory Arrangements) Amendment Bill 2026, the Counter-Terrorism Legislation Amendment Bill 2026 and the Passenger Movement Charge Amendment Bill 2026 stand referred to the Federation Chamber for further consideration.

As Deputy Speaker, put successive questions on amendments moved by the members for Kooyong and Canning to the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026, and presented a replacement explanatory memorandum for the bill.

Speaking in support of the Combatting Illicit Tobacco Bill 2026, argued that cutting tobacco excise would only increase smoking rates, and detailed the bill's move to strengthen proceeds-of-crime powers and information-sharing to target the criminal networks selling illicit tobacco, citing 66 daily smoking deaths, over 175 tobacco shop firebombings in three years and a 150 per cent rise in tobacco-related armed robberies in Victoria since February 2024, while also opposing calls to deregulate vaping.
